findings.message: Kanthal lists 2282 °F as the highest kiln temperature for coils in grooves; this kiln reaches 2345 °F. Kiln makers build cone 10 kilns this way, with shorter element life.
findings.reference: Kanthal key data for elements; electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S14]

findings.message: The elements draw 48.0 A hot at 240 V. At +5 % supply voltage (ANSI C84.1 Range A) that is 50.4 A, and 52.8 A while the wire is cold, against the 48 A continuous limit. Kiln makers rate kilns the same way.

The tool chose 8 elements of 10 AWG wire (2.59 mm): the fewest elements that work, each with the thickest wire whose coil fits its groove. Kanthal recommends wire of 3 mm or more for the longest life in grooves. 12 elements would take 8 AWG (3.26 mm); set elements: 12 in the design's electric heat to use them.
The elements alone can't hold the top temperature; in this hybrid the burners take over before then.
Electrical work must follow your local code and be checked by a licensed electrician. These results are engineering guidance, not an approved design.

working.formula: 0.8 × breaker rating (the breaker is 125% of a continuous load)

working.reference: NEC 210.20(A) continuous loads at 125%, as applied by L&L; electric-and-thermal.md §3 [S25]

working.formula: P = V·I
working.name: Power the circuit can supply

working.formula: 20 A up to 13.3 A; above that, 150 % of the kiln's current, or the next standard size up
working.name: Largest breaker allowed
working.reference: NEC 422.11(E), a single non-motor appliance, as reported; standard sizes 240.6(A); electric-and-thermal.md §3 [S23, S79]

working.formula: ρ_T = ρ20 · Ct

working.note: The wire is assumed to run 100 °C above the kiln; Ct changes little there.
working.reference: electric-and-thermal.md §1.1, §1.2, §1.4: Kanthal APM data sheet [S2], atmospheres [S9]

working.formula: d³ = 4·ρ_T·P² / (π²·U²·p)
working.name: Smallest wire for the surface-load limit
working.reference: Krueger Pottery, A-1 coils in grooves; electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S15]

working.name: Wire chosen
working.note: The fewest elements that work, then the thickest standard gauge (ASTM B258) for them: at or above the smallest diameter, with a coil that fits the groove at a pitch of 2–4 wire diameters. Thicker wire lasts longer (Kanthal).
working.reference: electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S9, S13]

working.formula: L = U²/P · (πd²/4) / ρ_T
working.name: Wire length per element

working.formula: p = P / (π·d·L)
working.name: Surface load
working.reference: Krueger Pottery, A-1 coils in grooves; electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S15]

working.formula: turns = L / (π·(D − d)); pitch = groove length / turns
working.name: Coil
working.reference: Kanthal, element in grooves; electric-and-thermal.md §1.6 [S13, S14]

working.name: Installed power per unit of chamber volume
working.note: For comparison, 7 cu ft cone 10 kilns from L&L and Skutt have about 1650–1720 W/ft³ (electric-and-thermal.md §7 [S73, S74]).

working.formula: P_installed / Q_loss
working.name: Installed power over steady loss at top temperature
working.note: Power above the loss is what heats the ware and walls near the top.

findings.message: Cost per firing needs a firing schedule and the heat stored in the walls and ware; that comes with the firing simulation (plan milestone M6).
Weld the frame and fit it before the arch form comes out: the steel is what holds the arch up.
The front wall is the door: bricked up, dry, for each firing. Lay the inner and outer courses together, staggered, with a header course two-thirds of the way up.
Side-mounted burners need a bag wall so the flames don't hit the ware: hard brick, first course solid in front of the burners.
Damper: a kiln shelf in a slot 16.5 in wide and one course high, about a foot above the top of the flue. Brace the chimney with angle at its corners and tie it to the kiln frame.

Three spy holes, 2¼ × 2½ in (a quarter brick), in the door: about 8 in above the floor (a course above any burner ports there), midway and near the top, a few inches off centre so they miss the shelf posts. Cone packs in the top and bottom, draw rings in the middle.

Arch bricks: Back wall, layer 1 from the inside, above the springline: about 4 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's curve; Door, layer 1 from the inside, above the springline: about 4 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's curve; Left wall, the skewback and fill on top: about 22 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's angle; Right wall, the skewback and fill on top: about 22 bricks by volume, cut to the arch's angle.
findings.reference: Arch and wedge shapes, 9-inch series; electric-and-thermal.md §5 [S54]

findings.message: The skewbacks and the fill beside the arch are drawn along the arch's radius at the springline and counted by volume. The skewback's face must match the arch: 60° to the horizontal here, 90° less half the arch's central angle (HarbisonWalker's 60° skews suit a 60° arch, its 48° skews one at 2.302 in/ft). The steel that takes the arch's thrust is in the frame.

Castable: cure 16–24 h above 60 °F kept damp, never let it freeze, and dry it out slowly before the first firing (for Mizzou: 75 °F/h with a ½ h hold per inch at 250, 500 and 1000 °F). Follow the maker's sheet for your castable.

Brick counts assume dry joints at the nominal 9 × 4½ × 2½ in size, a ⅛ in saw cut, and 10% extra for breakage. At the corners the side walls run through and the back and door fit between them, layer by layer.
